title: SEMEN, WASHING, AND RITUAL PURITY: THE BIBLE PASSAGE NOBODY VOLUNTEERS TO TEACH
paragraphs:
SEMEN, WASHING, AND RITUAL PURITY: THE BIBLE PASSAGE NOBODY VOLUNTEERS TO TEACH
Leviticus says a man who releases semen must wash and remain “unclean until evening.” But if you think that means sex is dirty, semen is sinful, or God is ashamed of the human body, you may have completely misunderstood one of the Bible’s most uncomfortable passages.
There are Bible passages people underline.
There are passages people frame and hang on walls.
There are verses printed on coffee mugs, stitched onto shirts, written inside wedding cards, and posted over sunsets on Facebook.
And then there is Leviticus 15.
Nobody seems to volunteer for that sermon.
Nobody walks into a Christian bookstore asking where the inspirational merchandise about bodily discharges is kept.
Yet there it is.
In the Bible.
Not hidden in some forbidden manuscript.
Not added by an embarrassed medieval theologian.
Right there in Scripture.
And perhaps our discomfort with it reveals something important—not about the Bible, but about us.
Because God is willing to speak about parts of embodied human existence that religious people sometimes prefer to pretend do not exist.
Leviticus 15:16 begins:
“וְאִישׁ כִּי־תֵצֵא מִמֶּנּוּ שִׁכְבַת־זָרַע…”
Ve’ish ki-tetze mimennu shikhvat-zara…
The central Hebrew expression is שִׁכְבַת־זָרַע — shikhvat zeraʿ, an expression referring to an emission of semen, literally built around the ideas of “lying” and “seed.”
The verse continues:
“וְרָחַץ בַּמַּיִם אֶת־כָּל־בְּשָׂרוֹ וְטָמֵא עַד־הָעָרֶב”
Verachatz bammayim et-kol-besaro, vetame ad-ha‘arev.
In straightforward English:
He is to wash his whole body with water and remain ritually impure until evening.
That last sentence is where centuries of unnecessary shame can begin if we read the Bible carelessly.
Because Scripture does not say:
“He has sinned.”
It does not say:
“God is disgusted with him.”
It does not say:
“His sexuality has made him morally corrupt.”
It says he becomes טָמֵא — tameʾ.
Ritually impure.
That distinction matters enormously.
In the world of Leviticus, “unclean” does not automatically mean “sinful.”
Read that again, especially if someone once used religious language to make you ashamed of having a human body.
Ritual impurity and moral guilt are not identical categories.
A person could become ritually impure through ordinary bodily circumstances without having committed a moral transgression.
That changes everything.

Leviticus 15 is concerned with bodily discharges. It discusses abnormal male discharge, seminal emission, menstruation, abnormal female bleeding, washing, waiting, and the boundaries surrounding Israel’s sanctuary.
The chapter eventually tells us why these regulations mattered so seriously: Israel was to be guarded from impurity because God’s tabernacle stood among them.
This is sacred-space language.
God had chosen to dwell among His people.
And approaching His sanctuary was not treated casually.
There were boundaries between common and holy, clean and unclean, ordinary human existence and the concentrated holiness associated with God’s dwelling place.
That means Leviticus 15:16 is not God announcing that semen is evil.
In fact, the next verses make that interpretation extremely difficult.
If semen gets onto clothing or leather, the affected material is washed and remains impure until evening.
Then comes verse 18.
A man and woman have sexual relations involving seminal emission, and both wash and remain impure until evening.
Notice what the passage does not do.
It does not condemn the married couple for having sex.
It does not command a sacrifice for sexual immorality merely because intercourse occurred.
It does not describe marital intimacy itself as rebellion against God.
Instead, it places the bodily event within Israel’s ritual purity system.
There is an enormous difference between saying, “Your body has entered a temporary ritual condition,” and saying, “You have committed moral evil.”
Confuse those categories and you can manufacture shame God never commanded.
And some people reading this know exactly what religious shame feels like.
Maybe nobody explained the difference to you.
Maybe Christianity was introduced to you mostly through warnings.
Don’t touch.
Don’t feel.
Don’t desire.
Don’t ask.
Don’t admit.
Don’t talk about your body.
And certainly don’t tell anyone what you are struggling with.
So you learned something churches rarely realize they are teaching.
You learned how to hide.
You learned how to smile while carrying questions you thought would disgust everybody in the room.
Maybe your struggle went beyond innocent questions.
Maybe pornography became the place you ran when loneliness became unbearable.
Maybe lust started quietly and became a prison.
Maybe masturbation became tangled with compulsion, fantasy, secrecy, shame, or habits you desperately wanted to escape.
Maybe sexual sin really did enter the picture.
If so, Scripture does not help us by pretending sin is harmless.
Jesus certainly did not.
Christ takes sexual holiness deeper than external behavior. He confronts lust within the heart. The apostles call believers away from sexual immorality and toward holiness.
Grace never requires us to rename darkness as light.
But neither does holiness require us to call everything about the human body dirty.
There is a difference between having a body and using that body sinfully.
There is a difference between biological function and lust.
There is a difference between ritual impurity under the Mosaic covenant and moral rebellion against God.
There is a difference between conviction and humiliation.
And somebody desperately needs that distinction tonight.
Because conviction says:
“Come home.”
Shame says:
“Hide.”
Conviction exposes the wound because God intends to heal.
Condemnation whispers that you are the wound and therefore should never let anyone see you.
One voice leads you toward Christ.
The other makes you run into the shadows.
And humanity has been running into shadows for a very long time.
Long before Leviticus.
Long before Israel.
Long before the tabernacle.
There was a garden.
There was nakedness without shame.
There was intimacy without corruption.
There was humanity standing before God with nothing to conceal.
Then sin entered.
And suddenly Adam and Eve realized they were naked.
They covered themselves.
They hid.
Listen carefully to the movement of the story.
Sin.
Shame.
Covering.
Hiding.
Then God came looking.
“Where are you?”
God was not confused about Adam’s GPS coordinates.
The question exposed a spiritual catastrophe.
Adam had moved from fellowship into hiding.
And humanity has been sewing fig leaves ever since.
Some fig leaves look religious.
Some look respectable.
Some look like Sunday clothes and Christian vocabulary.
Some look like browser histories being erased at 2:13 in the morning.
Some look like marriages where nobody tells the truth anymore.
Some look like pastors terrified somebody will discover they are struggling.
Some look like teenagers convinced God hates them because nobody ever explained the difference between temptation, bodily development, lust, ritual categories, and deliberate sin.
Some look like grown adults still carrying shame somebody handed them when they were fourteen.
And then Scripture does something astonishing.
It keeps moving toward Jesus.
The purity laws of Leviticus teach us that the presence of the holy God is not trivial.
God is not merely a spiritual accessory.
His holiness is not decorative.
Sin is not imaginary.
Defilement is not meaningless.
Human beings cannot stroll into divine holiness on whatever terms they invent.
But the biblical story does not end with humanity standing outside.
It moves toward a Savior who comes to us.
And when Jesus arrives, something breathtaking begins happening around purity.
People everyone else avoids start approaching Him.
Lepers.
Bleeding people.
Broken people.
People carrying scandal.
People carrying histories.
People carrying bodies that have failed them.
People carrying sins they cannot undo.
In Mark 5, a woman has suffered from bleeding for twelve years.
Twelve years.
Think about that.
Not twelve minutes of embarrassment.
Not twelve days.
Twelve years.
She has suffered physically and financially. She has spent what she had seeking help.
Then she moves through a crowd toward Jesus.
She touches His garment.
And instead of her uncleanness overpowering Christ, Christ’s power overwhelms her condition.
The bleeding stops.
Jesus does not recoil.
He does not say, “How dare you touch Me?”
He calls her:
“Daughter.”
Imagine how that word sounded after twelve years of suffering.
Daughter.
That is what Jesus does with people who have been reduced to their condition.
The crowd sees the problem.
Jesus sees the person.
Religion can sometimes turn people into labels.
Addict.
Impure.
Divorced.
Pornographer.
Adulterer.
Failure.
Backslider.
Dirty.
Jesus does not deny sin or suffering, but neither does He reduce human beings to their worst chapter.
He restores people.
And eventually He goes somewhere even more shocking.
To the cross.
There, the One who is truly clean stands where the unclean belong.
The sinless One bears sin.
The righteous One is numbered with transgressors.
The beloved Son enters our disgrace.
Jesus does not save us by pretending we were already clean.
He saves us by doing what we could never do for ourselves.
This is why Christianity is not fundamentally the story of dirty people learning how to scrub harder.
It is the story of a holy Savior cleansing people who could never cleanse themselves from sin.
Water could wash Israelite skin.
Time could bring ritual impurity to its appointed end.
Priestly procedures could restore ceremonial access where the Law prescribed them.
But soap cannot wash guilt from a conscience.
A shower cannot cleanse adultery.
A bath cannot remove pornography from the heart.
Water cannot erase hatred.
Religious performance cannot undo rebellion.
You need something deeper.
You need redemption.
You need forgiveness.
You need Christ.
The New Testament takes us there with extraordinary force.
Hebrews speaks about purification reaching the conscience and points us toward the blood of Christ.
First John declares that the blood of Jesus cleanses from sin.
Paul tells believers that some of them once lived in devastating forms of sin, and then comes one of the most beautiful reversals in Scripture:
“But you were washed…”
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Not because they successfully edited their past.
Not because nobody found out.
Not because their scandal suddenly became acceptable.
Because Jesus Christ intervened.
This is the Gospel Warrior heartbeat:
Not from scandal to pretending.
Not from scandal to public relations.
Not from scandal to religious camouflage.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe that sounds beautiful until your own scandal enters the sentence.
Then suddenly theology becomes personal.
What about what you watched?
What about what you did?
What about the affair?
What about the fantasy?
What about the person you used?
What about the years you wasted?
What about the secret account?
What about what happened behind the locked door?
What about the promises to God you broke again three days later?
What about the thing you cannot bring yourself to type into a comment because even seeing the words makes your stomach turn?
The Gospel does not tell you your sin does not matter.
The cross proves it matters more than you imagined.
But the cross also proves something else.
God’s mercy is greater than your ability to destroy yourself.
That does not mean consequences magically disappear.
It does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
It does not mean every broken relationship will automatically be restored.
Biblical grace is not permission to keep worshiping the thing that is killing you.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance.
Real repentance.
The kind that stops negotiating with darkness.
The kind that brings secrets into the light.
The kind that confesses.
The kind that seeks accountability.
The kind that cuts off access when necessary.
The kind that says, “Jesus, I cannot keep calling You Lord while protecting the very thing You are telling me to surrender.”
But repentance is not purchasing forgiveness with enough tears.
Repentance runs toward the Savior because grace has opened the door.
And perhaps that is why this strange passage about semen, washing, and ritual purity matters more than we thought.
It reminds us that the Bible is remarkably unafraid of embodied humanity.
God knows we bleed.
God knows we sweat.
God knows bodies produce fluids.
God invented human reproduction.
God designed marriage.
God created sexuality with purpose and boundaries.
And God also knows how sin can invade His gifts, distort desire, exploit bodies, enslave imagination, wound marriages, and turn intimacy into consumption.
He is neither embarrassed by your humanity nor indifferent to your holiness.
He wants all of you.
Not merely the church version.
Not merely the Facebook version.
Not merely the version holding a Bible in your profile picture.
You.
The person nobody else sees.
The thoughts you delete.
The history you conceal.
The appetite you keep feeding.
The wound underneath the appetite.
The loneliness underneath the behavior.
The shame underneath the smile.
Jesus does not stand outside your locked room shouting, “Clean yourself before I come in.”
He calls you into the light.
And yes, coming into the light can hurt.
Because light exposes.
But the same light that exposes the infection shows the surgeon where to heal.
So stop confusing hiding with holiness.
Somebody reading this has been hiding for years.
You love Jesus.
At least you believe you do.
But there is an area of your life you keep fencing off from Him.
You worship with it.
Sleep with it.
Wake up with it.
Delete it.
Confess it.
Return to it.
Hate it.
Miss it.
Promise to quit it.
Then hide it again.
And you are exhausted.
If that is you, perhaps your prayer tonight does not need impressive language.
Maybe it needs five words:
“Jesus, no more hiding. Help me.”
You do not have to publish graphic details of your struggle.
You do not owe strangers your private history.
But sometimes publicly admitting that you need Christ is the first crack in a wall secrecy has been building for years.
Someone reading the comments may discover hope because you were brave enough to admit that grace is still doing surgery.
Not because an algorithm needs another post.
Someone may believe bodily temptation means God hates them.
Someone may be confusing ritual impurity with moral guilt.
Someone else may actually be trapped in sexual sin and desperately needs to hear that grace does not mean surrendering to bondage—it means there is still a road home through Jesus Christ.
And when it does, come back and remember:
ritual impurity was not automatically moral guilt.
Human embodiment is not automatically sexual sin.
Sexual sin is real and must not be excused.
Repentance is necessary.
Grace is real.
Christ is sufficient.
And hiding is not your only option anymore.
If Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture more deeply, stay close to this ministry.
We are trying to build something deeper than inspirational scrolling.
We are saved by grace, not by purchasing access, supporting a ministry, sharing a post, or performing religious works.
But redeemed people can freely choose to support Gospel work out of gratitude, generosity, and a desire to help others hear truth.
But before you leave this page, remember the man in Leviticus.
He washed.
He waited.
Evening came.
His temporary ritual condition ended.
And remember the bleeding woman.
Twelve years.
Then Jesus.
Remember the sinners Paul described.
Then came those astonishing words:
“But you were washed.”
And now remember yourself.
Your story may contain pages you wish had never been written.
There may be stains you cannot erase by replaying them.
There may be consequences you still have to face.
There may be repentance you still need to make.
There may be help you need to seek.
There may be a confession that cannot remain postponed forever.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, your scandal does not possess the authority to write the final sentence.
Christ does.
So come out of hiding.
Bring the body.
Bring the questions.
Bring the temptation.
Bring the failure.
Bring the wounds.
Bring the guilt that actually is guilt.
Bring the shame that never belonged there.
Bring the secrets.
Bring the years.
Bring the shattered pieces.
Bring everything into the light of Christ.
Because the Savior who calls you to holiness is the same Savior who carried a cross for sinners.
And when Jesus cleanses what sin has stained, your worst chapter discovers it was never holding the pen.
